series.series_title: The Dog Who Never Stopped Waiting
series.throughline: Why did one dog keep returning to a Tokyo train station for almost ten years, and how did Japan remember him?

episodes.series_title: The Dog Who Never Stopped Waiting
episodes.episode_title: The Professor Who Never Came Home
episodes.youtube_title: The Dog Who Never Stopped Waiting (Part 1/3)
episodes.script: This dog waited for his dead owner for almost ten years. Hollywood later turned his story into a Richard Gere movie. His name was Hachiko, an Akita in Tokyo. Every day, he met his owner, Professor Hidesaburo Ueno, at Shibuya Station. Then, in May 1925, Ueno died suddenly at work. He was never coming home. Hachiko had lost his whole world. But nobody could explain that to a dog. And soon, Hachiko went back to the one place Ueno would never return to. Subscribe so you don't miss Part 2.
episodes.cliffhanger: Soon, Hachiko went back to the one place Ueno would never return to.
episodes.description: In 1925, a Tokyo professor went to work and never came home. His dog didn't understand. Would your dog wait for you?

episodes.series_title: The Dog Who Never Stopped Waiting
episodes.episode_title: Waiting at Shibuya Station
episodes.youtube_title: The Dog Who Never Stopped Waiting (Part 2/3)
episodes.script: Hachiko went back to the station every single day. In Part 1, his owner, Professor Ueno, died suddenly at work in 1925. Hachiko was passed between caretakers, but he kept returning to Shibuya Station, waiting for a train that never brought Ueno home. Some people kicked him and pushed him away. Then, in 1932, a newspaper told his story, and all of Japan fell in love with him. People brought him food. Teachers called him a lesson in loyalty. But in 1934, Hachiko got something most heroes only get after they die. Subscribe so you don't miss Part 3.
episodes.cliffhanger: In 1934, Hachiko got something most heroes only get after they die.
episodes.description: Hachiko kept going back to Shibuya Station long after his owner died, until a newspaper made him a national hero. Could you wait that long?

episodes.series_title: The Dog Who Never Stopped Waiting
episodes.episode_title: A Statue for a Living Dog
episodes.youtube_title: The Dog Who Never Stopped Waiting (Part 3/3)
episodes.script: Hachiko got to see his own statue. In Part 2, a newspaper story made the waiting dog famous across Japan. In April 1934, a bronze statue of Hachiko was unveiled at Shibuya Station, and Hachiko was there. Less than a year later, he died. He had kept coming back for almost ten years. His ashes were buried in the same cemetery as Ueno. And in 2015, the University of Tokyo unveiled a new statue: Hachiko leaping up to greet his owner, together again at last. Subscribe for a new true story every day.
episodes.description: A statue while he was still alive, and a reunion 80 years in the making. Did Hachiko's ending get you?

episodes.series_title: The Titanic Stewardess Who Wouldn't Sink
episodes.episode_title: The Crash Before the Iceberg
episodes.youtube_title: The Titanic Stewardess Who Wouldn't Sink (Part 1/3)
episodes.script: The Titanic wasn't the only disaster this stewardess survived. The movie Titanic shows just one of her three close calls at sea. Her name was Violet Jessop, born in Argentina to Irish parents. In 1911, she was a stewardess on the giant liner Olympic. That September, Olympic collided with a Royal Navy warship called the Hawke. Nobody died, and the damaged liner made it back to port. Then Violet was offered a job on Olympic's brand-new sister ship. It was called Titanic. And as Titanic sank, an officer put something unexpected into her arms. Subscribe so you don't miss Part 2.
episodes.cliffhanger: And as Titanic sank, an officer put something unexpected into her arms.
episodes.description: Before Titanic, stewardess Violet Jessop was aboard its sister ship when it crashed into a warship. Would you have taken the Titanic job after that?

episodes.series_title: The Titanic Stewardess Who Wouldn't Sink
episodes.episode_title: A Stranger's Baby in Lifeboat 16
episodes.youtube_title: The Titanic Stewardess Who Wouldn't Sink (Part 2/3)
episodes.script: The officer handed Violet a baby. In Part 1, Violet joined Titanic after its sister ship Olympic crashed into a warship. After the iceberg, she was ordered on deck to set an example for non-English speakers. Then, according to her memoir, an officer gave her a baby to look after. She carried it into Lifeboat 16. On the rescue ship Carpathia, a woman snatched the baby and ran off without a word. Nobody knows what became of that child. Four years later, Violet's lifeboat was dragged toward a sinking ship's propellers. Subscribe so you don't miss Part 3.
episodes.cliffhanger: Four years later, Violet's lifeboat was dragged toward a sinking ship's propellers.
episodes.description: On Titanic's last night, an officer handed Violet Jessop a baby, and on the rescue ship a stranger took it and ran. Who do you think that woman was?

episodes.episode_title: The Third Sister Ship
episodes.youtube_title: The Titanic Stewardess Who Wouldn't Sink (Part 3/3)
episodes.script: Violet jumped out of a lifeboat to escape spinning propellers. In Part 2, Violet survived Titanic, holding a stranger's baby in her lifeboat. By 1916, she was a nurse aboard Britannic, Titanic's other sister, now a World War One hospital ship. It struck a German mine in the Aegean Sea and sank in under an hour. As lifeboats launched, the still-turning propellers began pulling them in. Violet jumped into the sea and suffered a serious head injury. She survived that too. Today, she's remembered as unsinkable. Three sister ships, three disasters, and Violet survived every one. Subscribe for a new true story every day.
episodes.description: Violet Jessop was aboard for a collision, the Titanic and a wartime mine, all on sister ships. Would you ever go back to sea after that?

episodes.script: A packed jet lost both engines just minutes after takeoff. And its captain would pick the strangest runway in New York. It was a freezing January afternoon, and the plane had just left LaGuardia Airport. Then it flew straight into a flock of Canada geese. Birds were sucked into both engines, and the power died. Now the jet was gliding, low over one of the biggest cities on Earth. The pilots had only minutes to find somewhere to land. Captain Sully Sullenberger chose the frigid Hudson River. Subscribe so you don't miss Part 2.
episodes.cliffhanger: Captain Sully Sullenberger chose the frigid Hudson River.
episodes.description: A flock of geese, two dead engines, and a jet gliding over New York City with minutes to spare. Where would you have tried to land?

episodes.series_title: Both Engines Died Over New York City
episodes.episode_title: The Passengers Who Waited on the Wings
episodes.youtube_title: Both Engines Died Over New York City (Part 2/3)
episodes.script: A jet full of people came gliding down onto a frigid river. In Part 1, geese knocked out both engines over New York City. The pilots set the plane down on the Hudson, and it floated. Cold water began pouring into the back of the cabin. Passengers climbed out onto the wings and waited in the freezing wind. Within minutes, ferry boats raced over and pulled people aboard. Every one of the 155 people on board survived. But investigators later tested whether the plane could have reached a runway instead. Subscribe so you don't miss Part 3.
episodes.cliffhanger: But investigators later tested whether the plane could have reached a runway instead.
episodes.description: The plane floated, water poured in, and passengers stood on the wings in the freezing wind until ferries arrived. Would you have stayed calm out there?

episodes.series_title: Both Engines Died Over New York City
episodes.episode_title: The Simulator Tests That Questioned Sully
episodes.youtube_title: Both Engines Died Over New York City (Part 3/3)
episodes.script: Computer tests later suggested the jet might have reached an airport. In Part 2, all 155 people survived a Hudson River landing. Pilots flew the same emergency in flight simulators. About half of them made it back to a runway. But they turned back instantly, with no time to think. When investigators added about half a minute for thinking, the simulated flight crashed. They concluded the river gave everyone the best chance to survive. The movie Sully later built its drama around those tests. The runway nobody would pick was the right one. Subscribe for a new true story every day.
episodes.description: Simulator pilots sometimes made it back to a runway, until investigators added time to think. The movie Sully turned those tests into drama. Did the captain make the right call?

episodes.episode_title: The Bayonne Bleeder Gets His Shot
episodes.youtube_title: The Real Rocky Lost to Muhammad Ali (Part 1/3)
episodes.script: The boxer who inspired Rocky actually lost to Muhammad Ali. And round nine of that fight still starts arguments. His name was Chuck Wepner, a New Jersey club fighter nicknamed the Bayonne Bleeder. He once said he needed 328 stitches over his career. In 1975, he got a shot at Ali's heavyweight title. Bookmakers made him a massive underdog. Ali's purse was more than ten times bigger than his. Then, in the ninth round, the champion ended up on the canvas. Subscribe so you don't miss Part 2.
episodes.cliffhanger: Then, in the ninth round, the champion ended up on the canvas.
episodes.description: A New Jersey club fighter called the Bayonne Bleeder got a title shot against Muhammad Ali. Would you have bet on him?

episodes.series_title: The Real Rocky Lost to Muhammad Ali
episodes.episode_title: Knockdown or Stepped-On Foot
episodes.youtube_title: The Real Rocky Lost to Muhammad Ali (Part 2/3)
episodes.script: Chuck Wepner knocked down Muhammad Ali, at least officially. In Part 1, a club fighter nicknamed the Bayonne Bleeder got a title shot against Ali. The knockdown came in the ninth round. But Ali said Wepner had stepped on his foot and pushed him. Film of the fight backed Ali up, though Wepner always insisted it was real. Wepner kept fighting anyway. The referee finally stopped it with just 19 seconds left in the final round. Wepner needed 23 stitches. And a little-known actor watching that fight was about to write a Best Picture winner. Subscribe so you don't miss Part 3.
episodes.cliffhanger: And a little-known actor watching that fight was about to write a Best Picture winner.
episodes.description: Wepner put Ali on the canvas and lasted into the final round, but was it really a knockdown or a stepped-on foot? What do you think?

episodes.series_title: The Real Rocky Lost to Muhammad Ali
episodes.episode_title: From Losing Fighter to Best Picture
episodes.youtube_title: The Real Rocky Lost to Muhammad Ali (Part 3/3)
episodes.script: Rocky's script was written right after Wepner lost. In Part 2, Wepner lasted until the final round before the referee stopped it. Sylvester Stallone, then a little-known actor, had watched it. He later said Wepner seemed to have no chance. Soon after, Stallone wrote Rocky in less than four days. Unlike Wepner, his underdog goes the distance. Rocky won Best Picture. Stallone at first denied Wepner was the inspiration, but later admitted it. Wepner sued him in 2003, and they settled out of court. He lost the title fight, but inspired the ultimate underdog. Subscribe for a new true story every day.
episodes.description: Stallone watched Wepner lose to Ali, then wrote Rocky in days. Did Wepner deserve credit for the ultimate underdog story?

episodes.series_title: Can Wolves Really Change Rivers?
episodes.episode_title: The Park That Lost Its Wolves
episodes.youtube_title: Can Wolves Really Change Rivers? (Part 1/3)
episodes.script: A viral video claims wolves changed the rivers of Yellowstone. To test it, you have to go back a century. Wolves once roamed the park, hunting elk across its valleys. People saw them as pests, and even park rangers hunted them down. By the late 1920s, the last wolves in the park were gone. Without them, elk herds grazed the riverbanks with little to fear. Young willows and aspens were chewed down year after year. Then, about 70 years later, wolves from Canada were brought back. Subscribe so you don't miss Part 2.
episodes.cliffhanger: Then, about 70 years later, wolves from Canada were brought back.
episodes.description: Yellowstone's wolves were wiped out, and the park changed without them. Then wolves from Canada were brought back. Should predators be brought back?

episodes.series_title: Can Wolves Really Change Rivers?
episodes.episode_title: The Wolves Come Home
episodes.youtube_title: Can Wolves Really Change Rivers? (Part 2/3)
episodes.script: Fourteen wolves from Canada were set free in Yellowstone. In Part 1, people wiped out the park's wolves by the late 1920s. The first wolves arrived in 1995, and more followed a year later. The wolves hunted elk, and elk numbers fell sharply. Scientists reported willows and aspens growing taller in places. Beaver colonies grew from one to nine in about a decade. It became one of the most famous comeback stories in nature. But the wolves weren't the only hunters killing Yellowstone's elk. Subscribe so you don't miss Part 3.
episodes.cliffhanger: But the wolves weren't the only hunters killing Yellowstone's elk.
episodes.description: Wolves returned to Yellowstone, elk numbers fell and beavers came back. It became a famous comeback story. Would you have brought them back?

episodes.series_title: Can Wolves Really Change Rivers?
episodes.episode_title: Wolves Did Not Do It Alone
episodes.youtube_title: Can Wolves Really Change Rivers? (Part 3/3)
episodes.script: The famous claim that wolves changed rivers has a big problem. In Part 2, elk numbers fell and willows grew after wolves returned. But cougars, bears and hunters outside the park were killing elk too. Later studies found the willow gains were smaller and patchier than claimed. In dry spots, willows barely grew, even with fewer elk around. Water, and the beavers that hold it back, mattered too. Many streams changed so much without beavers that they haven't bounced back. Wolves changed Yellowstone. They just didn't do it alone. Subscribe for a new true story every day.
episodes.description: Wolves got the credit for healing Yellowstone, but scientists say bears, hunters, water and beavers played big roles too. Did you believe the viral video?

episodes.series_title: He Crossed the Pacific on a Raft of Logs
episodes.episode_title: Six Men, Nine Logs, and No Engine
episodes.youtube_title: He Crossed the Pacific on a Raft of Logs (Part 1/3)
episodes.script: Six men tried crossing the Pacific on a raft of logs. They set out to prove an idea most experts had already rejected. The idea was that ancient South Americans could have reached Polynesia. So a Norwegian explorer, Thor Heyerdahl, copied the rafts of ancient South America. Nine giant balsa logs, tied together with rope, and no engine at all. They pushed off from Peru and let the ocean currents carry them west. Ahead lay more than 4,000 miles of open Pacific. And a coral reef was waiting at the very end. Subscribe so you don't miss Part 2.
episodes.cliffhanger: And a coral reef was waiting at the very end.
episodes.description: In 1947, six men set off from Peru on a balsa raft to prove an idea most experts had rejected. Would you have climbed aboard?

episodes.series_title: He Crossed the Pacific on a Raft of Logs
episodes.episode_title: The Raft That Crashed Onto a Coral Reef
episodes.youtube_title: He Crossed the Pacific on a Raft of Logs (Part 2/3)
episodes.script: After more than three months adrift, the raft smashed into a reef. In Part 1, six men set out from Peru on a raft of balsa logs. They caught flying fish, and met sharks and whales along the way. Then, near a Polynesian island called Raroia, the raft crashed onto the reef. All six men made it ashore on a tiny, empty island. They had crossed about 4,300 miles in 101 days. Heyerdahl's film of the trip even won an Oscar. But scientists still said his big idea was wrong. Subscribe so you don't miss Part 3.
episodes.cliffhanger: But scientists still said his big idea was wrong.
episodes.description: Sharks, whales, and a crash landing on a coral reef after 101 days at sea, and his film of it won an Oscar. So why did scientists still say he was wrong?

episodes.series_title: He Crossed the Pacific on a Raft of Logs
episodes.episode_title: The DNA Link Kon-Tiki Hinted At
episodes.youtube_title: He Crossed the Pacific on a Raft of Logs (Part 3/3)
episodes.script: Hidden in Polynesian DNA was a surprise link to South America. In Part 2, the Kon-Tiki raft crossed the Pacific, but experts still doubted Heyerdahl. Most scientists say Polynesians came from Asia, sailing east across the ocean. So his big idea was mostly wrong. But in 2020, a large DNA study found Native American ancestry in some Polynesians. The two peoples mixed around 800 years ago. Researchers think Polynesian sailors probably reached South America, though a drifting raft isn't ruled out. Heyerdahl may have had the direction wrong, but the contact was real. Subscribe for a new true story every day.
episodes.description: A 2020 DNA study found Native American ancestry in some Polynesians, centuries before Europeans arrived. The 2012 movie Kon-Tiki retold the raft trip. Who do you think sailed to whom?

episodes.youtube_title: The Eiffel Tower Was Supposed to Come Down (Part 1/3)
episodes.script: The Eiffel Tower was never meant to still be standing. It was built as the centerpiece of the 1889 World's Fair in Paris. At over 300 meters, it became the tallest structure in the world. But it only had a permit for 20 years. Before it was even finished, famous artists attacked it in a Paris newspaper. They called it useless and monstrous, like a giant black smokestack. When the permit ran out, the city could tear it down. And what saved it was something nobody could see. Subscribe so you don't miss Part 2.
episodes.cliffhanger: And what saved it was something nobody could see.
episodes.description: Famous artists called it monstrous, and its permit only lasted 20 years. Would you have voted to tear the Eiffel Tower down?

episodes.series_title: The Eiffel Tower Was Supposed to Come Down
episodes.episode_title: The Invisible Thing That Saved the Eiffel Tower
episodes.youtube_title: The Eiffel Tower Was Supposed to Come Down (Part 2/3)
episodes.script: Invisible radio waves saved the Eiffel Tower from being torn down. In Part 1, the tower only had a permit for 20 years. Gustave Eiffel kept a private apartment near the top, and filled the tower with experiments. He paid for wireless radio tests, with an antenna at the very top. Soon its signals could reach thousands of miles. When the permit ran out in 1909, the tower was too useful to lose. Paris let it stay. Then war came, and the tower began listening in on the enemy. Subscribe so you don't miss Part 3.
episodes.cliffhanger: Then war came, and the tower began listening in on the enemy.
episodes.description: Gustave Eiffel turned his tower into a giant science experiment, and radio made it too useful to demolish. Did you know the tower was saved by radio?

episodes.series_title: The Eiffel Tower Was Supposed to Come Down
episodes.episode_title: The Eiffel Tower and the Dancer Accused of Spying
episodes.youtube_title: The Eiffel Tower Was Supposed to Come Down (Part 3/3)
episodes.script: The Eiffel Tower helped put a famous dancer on trial for spying. In Part 2, radio waves saved the tower from being torn down. During World War One, its radio station listened in on enemy messages. In 1917, it caught coded German messages about a secret agent. France matched that agent to the dancer Mata Hari, and arrested her. But those messages used a code the Germans knew France had already broken. Some historians think she was set up. The tower Paris nearly tore down became the city's secret ear. Subscribe for a new true story every day.
episodes.description: Radio messages caught by the Eiffel Tower helped put Mata Hari on trial, but the code may have been a trap. Was she a real spy or a scapegoat?

episodes.series_title: The Cow Framed for the Great Chicago Fire
episodes.episode_title: The Night a Cow Took the Blame
episodes.youtube_title: The Cow Framed for the Great Chicago Fire (Part 1/3)
episodes.script: A cow took the blame for burning down Chicago. In 1871, a fire started near the O'Leary family's barn. The summer had been bone dry, and strong winds drove the flames into the heart of the city. It burned for about a day and a half, until rain finally came. About 300 people died, and about 100,000 lost their homes. Then came the story everyone remembers. Catherine O'Leary's cow supposedly kicked over a lantern and started it all. But one of the reporters who spread that story would later make a confession. Subscribe so you don't miss Part 2.
episodes.cliffhanger: But one of the reporters who spread that story would later make a confession.
episodes.description: A cow and a lantern took the blame for the Great Chicago Fire, but one reporter had a secret. Did you learn the cow story in school?

episodes.series_title: The Cow Framed for the Great Chicago Fire
episodes.episode_title: The Reporter's Confession
episodes.youtube_title: The Cow Framed for the Great Chicago Fire (Part 2/3)
episodes.script: The cow blamed for burning Chicago was probably framed by reporters. In Part 1, the Great Chicago Fire killed about 300 people, and a cow got blamed. Decades later, a reporter named Michael Ahern made a confession. He said he and other reporters invented the whole cow story. An official inquiry found no proof Catherine O'Leary caused the fire. Historians still don't know exactly how it started. In 1997, Chicago's city council officially cleared her and her cow. But that same night, a far deadlier fire was raging, and almost nobody remembers it. Subscribe so you don't miss Part 3.
episodes.cliffhanger: But that same night, a far deadlier fire was raging, and almost nobody remembers it.
episodes.description: The cow and lantern story made Catherine O'Leary infamous, until a reporter confessed. Should history apologize to her?

episodes.series_title: The Cow Framed for the Great Chicago Fire
episodes.episode_title: The Deadlier Fire Nobody Remembers
episodes.youtube_title: The Cow Framed for the Great Chicago Fire (Part 3/3)
episodes.script: America's deadliest wildfire burned on the very same night. In Part 2, a reporter admitted the Chicago cow story was invented. While Chicago burned, a firestorm tore through the forests around Peshtigo, Wisconsin. Survivors described a whirl of fire that tossed rail cars and houses. Many people escaped into the river. Somewhere between 1,200 and 2,500 people died, far more than in Chicago. But big-city Chicago and its cow legend grabbed the headlines. Even Peshtigo's records burned, so the true toll is still unknown. Chicago got the legend. Peshtigo was nearly forgotten. Subscribe for a new true story every day.
episodes.description: The same night Chicago burned, a far deadlier firestorm hit Peshtigo, Wisconsin. Had you ever heard of it?

episodes.series_title: What Finding Nemo Got Wrong About Clownfish
episodes.episode_title: Living Inside a Home Full of Stingers
episodes.youtube_title: What Finding Nemo Got Wrong About Clownfish (Part 1/3)
episodes.script: Real clownfish make their home inside an animal armed with stingers. Finding Nemo showed that part, but it skipped the strangest rules of clownfish life. Sea anemones are covered in stinging cells that keep predators away. Clownfish nestle right between the tentacles. Their secret is a coat of slimy mucus that doesn't set off the stings. In return, clownfish pick off parasites and fan fresh water over their host. And each clownfish group follows a strict ranking by size. But the rule for who's in charge would have turned Nemo's family upside down. Subscribe so you don't miss Part 2.
episodes.cliffhanger: But the rule for who's in charge would have turned Nemo's family upside down.
episodes.description: Clownfish live inside an animal covered in stingers, and they never get stung. Which ocean animal would you want as a roommate?

episodes.series_title: What Finding Nemo Got Wrong About Clownfish
episodes.episode_title: The Dad Who Would Have Become the Boss
episodes.youtube_title: What Finding Nemo Got Wrong About Clownfish (Part 2/3)
episodes.script: The boss of every clownfish family is its biggest female. In Part 1, clownfish survive inside stinging anemones thanks to a coat of slimy mucus. Her partner is the second-biggest fish, a male. When the female dies, her mate turns female. Then the biggest fish waiting in line becomes the new male. Scientists found the switch starts in the brain, long before the body catches up. So in real life, Nemo's dad would have become the new female in charge. But the movie was also blamed for a clownfish buying craze scientists later tested. Subscribe so you don't miss Part 3.
episodes.cliffhanger: But the movie was also blamed for a clownfish buying craze scientists later tested.
episodes.description: In a real clownfish family, the dad doesn't stay a dad when the female is gone. Did you know fish could do this?

episodes.series_title: What Finding Nemo Got Wrong About Clownfish
episodes.episode_title: Did the Movie Really Empty the Reefs?
episodes.youtube_title: What Finding Nemo Got Wrong About Clownfish (Part 3/3)
episodes.script: Scientists checked if Finding Nemo really sparked a clownfish buying spree. In Part 2, a real clownfish dad turns female when the mother dies. For years, news stories blamed the film for emptying reefs. An Oxford team checked online searches, aquarium visits and sales from a major fish importer. The data didn't show the film driving up clownfish demand. People mostly looked up information instead. And that famous escape down a drain? Flushed fish are usually killed by shock, sewage or treatment plants long before the sea. Turns out, the real clownfish was stranger than the cartoon. Subscribe for a new true story every day.

episodes.script: Two climbers may have topped Everest almost 30 years before anyone else. And the proof could still be frozen somewhere on the mountain. It was 1924, and nobody had ever stood on the highest point on Earth. British climbers George Mallory and Sandy Irvine made a final push for the top. A teammate far below spotted them high on the ridge, still climbing. Then clouds swept in and hid them from view. They never came back. Seventy-five years later, a search team found one of them on the mountain. Subscribe so you don't miss Part 2.
episodes.cliffhanger: Seventy-five years later, a search team found one of them on the mountain.
episodes.description: Two climbers were last seen high on Everest's ridge before clouds hid them, decades before the first confirmed ascent. Do you think they made it?

episodes.script: The climber found on Everest was George Mallory, and something was missing. In Part 1, two climbers vanished near the top of Everest. His body lay on the north face, with injuries that pointed to a fall. His snow goggles were in his pocket, a hint they were climbing down late. He had reportedly planned to leave a photo of his wife on the summit. That photo wasn't with him. The pair also carried a small camera that might prove it. That camera is still missing, but a century later, the ice gave up a clue. Subscribe so you don't miss Part 3.

episodes.youtube_title: The Climbers Who Vanished Near Everest's Top (Part 3/3)
episodes.script: A century later, Irvine's name melted out of Everest's ice. In Part 2, Mallory was found, but not the camera that might prove the summit. In 2024, a National Geographic team searched a glacier below the north face. They found an old boot and sock melting out of the ice, with remains inside. The sock had Irvine's name sewn into it. His family offered DNA to confirm it was him. No camera turned up, but the team says the search area is now smaller. Everest still won't say who stood on top first.
